tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 600000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

content.content:
1	# Issue #230: a browser page on the remote port, investigation notes
2	
3	Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md (84 lines, nothing about the remote port;
4	its lesson is the action/effect core, a fake for every port, and "spike
5	risky technology first"), docs/remote-client.md §§0–5, design.md "Trust
6	boundary" (l.219) and the start of "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (l.3107),
7	plus the code below. Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at
8	7fe8949. There is no `web/` directory yet.
9	
10	## The record first: what is on disk, and how it comes back
11	
12	- **No new record kind and no `model.rs` change is needed.** A browser is
13	  one more `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`: `id`, `name`,
14	  `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`) in
15	  `<data dir>/devices.json`. That file is a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>`
16	  with no schema version (`RemoteFiles::load_devices`/`save_devices`,
17	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-86`), written atomically by
18	  `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/core/remote.rs:121-125`). The name comes
19	  from `/pair`'s `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`), cut to 64 chars
20	  in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). So "Safari on
21	  iPhone" can be the page's own `device_name` with no host change. If
22	  the plan wants a `kind` (browser or native) on the device, it is an
23	  additive `#[serde(default)]` field in a file that has no version.
24	- **Rehydration** is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded { identity, devices,
25	  rotated }` (`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back at
26	  launch. A token is checked by hash against them on every request
27	  (`authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3125-3153`; `device_by_token`,
28	  `src/core/remote.rs:145-147`). Revoke (`RevokeDevice`,
29	  `src/core/remote.rs:86-92`) and scope change (`:93-100`) apply on the
30	  next request, and revoke closes the device's socket (test
31	  `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, `tests/remote.rs:2892`).
32	- **The pairing window is not durable** (`PairingWindow` in core state:
33	  code, scope, `until`, failures; `OpenPairing`/`ClosePairing`/
34	  `PairingFailed`/`Paired`, `src/core/remote.rs:46-73`). The QR is built
35	  in the UI from it (`src/ui/remote.rs:155-173`). Changing JSON to a URL
36	  is a change to that `json!` call and to the "Copy invite" text (`:199-206`),
37	  not to any record.
38	- **The page itself is not a record.** It is static bytes compiled in
39	  (`include_str!`). On the device, what persists is the token, plus
40	  whatever the page keeps to say "identity changed". Decision 2 picks
41	  where that is. The browser also keeps its certificate exception per
42	  host. The host keeps nothing new per browser beyond the device record.
43	- **Identity** (`identity.json`, `Identity` at `src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`,
44	  `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at `:17`). It holds the certificate
45	  (base64 DER) and `spki_sha256`. The certificate is made by
46	  `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) with
47	  `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`: **no subjectAltName at
48	  all**, a CN of `Switchboard <server_id>`, rcgen's default validity
49	  (the comment says `not_after` is the year 4096), and no EKU set
50	  explicitly. The native clients pin the SPKI and ignore names, so this
51	  never mattered. A browser checks names and validity. Changing the
52	  certificate (adding SANs for the LAN address or a `.local` name, or a
53	  bounded validity) changes nothing the pin sees if the key is reused
54	  (the SPKI is the same, §5). But the certificate is stored in
55	  `identity.json`, so reissuing it means writing that file, and an
56	  address that moves would need another reissue.
57	
58	## What the code does today, piece by piece
59	
60	### The listener (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)
61	
62	- `read_request` (`:444-513`) keeps the method, the path, the query
63	  (undecoded), the body, `bearer` (`Authorization: Bearer`, `:487-491`)
64	  and `upgrade` (`Sec-WebSocket-Key` when `Upgrade: websocket`,
65	  `:492-495`). It throws away every other header. **It does not read
66	  `Cookie`, `Origin`, `User-Agent`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Host`,
67	  `If-None-Match` or `Accept`.** Either token transport in decision 2
68	  needs a new `RemoteRequest` field. That struct is in
69	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:359-372`, which is not under `ports/`, but
70	  `tests/remote.rs` builds requests and should be checked.
71	- `respond` (`:530-552`) always writes `Content-Type: application/json`
72	  and `Connection: keep-alive`, nothing else. It has no CSP, no
73	  Cache-Control, no Set-Cookie and no other content type. `RemoteReply`
74	  (`:388-393`) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. Static files and a
75	  cookie on `/pair` therefore need `RemoteReply` (or a separate
76	  connection-thread path) to carry headers. `respond_upgrade`
77	  (`:519-527`) writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A browser that offered
78	  a subprotocol fails the handshake if the server does not echo one
79	  (that is a question below, not checked).
80	- Pools and windows: `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12`
81	  (`:567-568`). A stream past the 4 is dropped at accept (`:699-706`). A
82	  connection moves pools only when a reply says `authenticated: true`
83	  (`:834-849`). `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` is 5 s (`:570`), and the first
84	  request line has the same deadline. `IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 s (`:573`).
85	  The rate windows exist only for `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and
86	  `/api/v1/info` (60/min) (`:583-587`, `Limits::limited` `:629-640`).
87	  Any other path, a static one included, is unlimited and goes to the
88	  frame. What this means for a page load: a browser opens several
89	  parallel connections and keeps them alive. Static GETs leave a
90	  connection in the unauthenticated pool for up to 30 s idle. A
91	  failed TLS handshake (the certificate warning) also holds a slot until
92	  it ends. **The pool of 4 is what an unpaired page load competes for.**
93	  Once paired, each fetch with the cookie or token moves its connection
94	  to the paired pool. The test `stalled_strangers_fill_their_own_pool_and_never_a_paired_clients`
95	  (`tests/remote.rs:3226`) is the existing model for that behaviour.
96	- The frame drain: `port.poll(DRAIN_PER_PASS)` then `serve_remote` for
97	  each (`src/app.rs:1585-1597`). The connection thread answers 429/503/504
98	  without the frame (`src/adapters/remote.rs:787-833`). Static bytes
99	  could be answered on the connection thread the same way (they need no
100	  core state), or on the frame through `serve_remote`. §4.1 "the frame
101	  does core state only" leans toward the connection thread. Not decided
102	  here.
103	
104	### The router (`src/app.rs`)
105	
106	- `serve_remote` (`:3017-3121`) refuses any path without the `/api/v1/`
107	  prefix with 404 `not_found` (`:3023-3025`). Then it answers `info` and
108	  `pair` unauthenticated (`:3027-3031`), authenticates, and handles
109	  `events` (`:3036-3038`) and the allowlist. The static paths would be a
110	  new arm before the prefix match, and they are the third thing served
111	  before pairing (§5's rule, `docs/remote-client.md` l.390 in the
112	  section, "Require pairing before anything but `/info` and `/pair`").
113	- `authenticate` (`:3125-3153`) knows only `request.bearer`. Both its
114	  refusals have the code `unauthorized`, with different messages: "pair
115	  this device first" (no token) and "the token is not known; pair again"
116	  (revoked, rotated, or never valid). **A page cannot tell "revoked"
117	  from "never paired" by the code.** With an HttpOnly cookie, the page
118	  cannot even see whether it holds a token. The "revoked" state in the
119	  issue needs either a distinct code (additive) or a non-secret marker
120	  the page keeps itself (for example, "I paired with server X as device
121	  Y").
122	- `remote_subscribe` (`:2723-2758`) requires `request.upgrade` and a
123	  device. It does not check `Origin`. Neither does anything else.
124	- `remote_pair` (`:3606-3674`) compares the body's `spki_sha256` with the
125	  host's own, then the code, uppercased. It counts a failure on either
126	  (`PairingFailed`). It answers `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` in
127	  the envelope. A cookie would be set here.
128	- `remote_info` (`:3568-3600`) carries `spki_sha256`, `server_name`,
129	  `capabilities`, `version`, `pairing_open`, but not the device's scope
130	  (it is unauthenticated). The header's "scope" comes from the `/pair`
131	  reply, and after that from nowhere: **no endpoint today tells a device
132	  its current scope**. A scope change in the dialog is invisible until a
133	  `control` command is refused. The Swift client has the same gap.
134	- `refuse` (`:3754-3772`) logs method and path, never the query. A
135	  `GET /?code=…` that reached the router would not log the code. Any
136	  new static handler must keep that true.
137	
138	### The session list and the excerpt
139	
140	- `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:636-688`) has `kind`, `card` (the
141	  card's word), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `liveness`,
142	  `trust_question`, `prompt_refusal`, `last_stop_at_ms`,
143	  `last_activity_ms`. **It has no excerpt or last-message field.** The
144	  §4.3 text (l.291 of the spec section) calls the card's one-line excerpt
145	  "`last_message` from the `Stop` hook on the record, a field of the
146	  session's metadata". That field is not on the wire, and `grep` finds no
147	  `last_message` in `control/src/lib.rs` or `src/app.rs`. The headset
148	  fills its compact card by fetching `sessions/{id}/last-response` per
149	  session (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`). So
150	  either the page does the same (N requests and N watches, against a
151	  watch set capped at 128), or the issue's "No new read model unless the
152	  page cannot do without one" is tested right here.
153	- Grouped by project: `GET projects` then `GET projects/{id}/sessions`
154	  each, or `GET waiting` for the waiting set. That is what the headset
155	  does. Worker records are hidden unless `?scope=all` (`hide_workers`,
156	  `:3116-3118`).
157	- The session view: `last-response` for a Claude session, `screen`
158	  otherwise. Both are content keys that need `watch` frames on the
159	  socket for `changed` (§4.4 "Watch frames"). The page must speak
160	  `watch`/`unwatch`, wait for `watching`, then fetch.
161	- Reply box: `POST sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}` under `control`
162	  (`remote_command`, `:3159`). The page makes the op (needs
163	  `crypto.randomUUID`, which only exists in a secure context; see
164	  questions) and follows §4.5's `/ops/{op}` rule on a timeout.
165	
166	### Pairing UI and the text paths
167	
168	- QR payload: `src/ui/remote.rs:160-166`, a JSON object with
169	  `addresses` holding at most one `ip:port` from `remote::local_address()`
170	  (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962-970`, the outward route's source
171	  address). An IPv6 result would need brackets in a URL. The address is
172	  whatever the route picks, not necessarily the one the phone reaches.
173	- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` decodes JSON only
174	  (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:93-116`).
175	  `switchboard-remote pair '<invite json>'` or `pair <host:port> <code>
176	  <spki>` (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:12-13,
177	  107-125`). `PairingInvite` is used by `ConnectionManager.swift`,
178	  `BrowserView.swift` and eight test files under `client/Tests`. Taking a
179	  URL means `parse` tries URL first (`URLComponents`, `code`/`key`/`id`)
180	  and JSON second. `addresses` comes from the URL's host and port.
181	- The README dev-aid text (l.265-278) documents "Copy invite" as the QR
182	  text and `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`. It must change with
183	  the payload.
184	- The script line `pairing <code>` (README l.278, `src/script.rs`) opens
185	  a window with a known code. That is enough to drive the page by hand
186	  against a test data dir.
187	
188	### Tests that exist and what extends
189	
190	- `tests/remote.rs` speaks raw HTTP/1.1 over a pinned rustls client
191	  (`http`, `:245-296`). It reads `Content-Length` only and keeps no other
192	  header, so header assertions (CSP, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie,
193	  Content-Type) need it to return headers. The relevant neighbours are
194	  `info_is_served_to_anyone_and_every_other_read_is_refused_unpaired`
195	  (`:426`), `the_allowlist_refuses_everything_else_with_no_side_effect`
196	  (`:682`), `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` (`:1406`),
197	  `subscribe_at` (`:1960`) and `the_client_fixtures_decode_on_both_sides`
198	  (`:1829`, `client/Fixtures`).
199	- "Every path the page references is served" can be a test over the
200	  embedded strings. The page is plain JS with no runner in the tree, so
201	  its logic (query parse, `replaceState`, revision reconcile) is
202	  untested unless the plan adds a JS test harness, which the issue rules
203	  out as a dependency. The page's protocol logic is therefore checked
204	  only by hand.
205	- CI runs on Linux. `include_str!` of `web/*` is portable.
206	
207	## Things the issue asserts that the tree contradicts or leaves open
208	
209	- "Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused": true (`src/app.rs:3023`), but
210	  on the frame, after the request was queued (so it costs inbox space),
211	  not at the connection thread.
212	- "the one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire (above).
213	- "the device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
214	  pairing (above).
215	- "'revoked' said plainly": the refusal code does not distinguish it
216	  (above).
217	- The `key` check in the page compares the URL's key with what `/info`
218	  says. A page cannot read the TLS certificate it is talking over, so
219	  this proves only that the host *claims* that key. A relay forwards
220	  `/info` faithfully, and the host's own `spki_sha256` check in
221	  `remote_pair` (`:3639-3647`) is fed by the page's body, which is the
222	  impostor's page under a relay. What it does catch is a genuine page on
223	  the wrong genuine host (a second installation at that address or
224	  port, or a rotated key). The issue says roughly this. The tree adds
225	  that §5's sentence "the host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is
226	  not its own, so a relayed request … fails" does not hold for a
227	  browser, and the spec text must say so.
228	- Cookies are scoped by host, not by port. Two Switchboard instances on
229	  one Mac (`SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`, design §3.1) and any other HTTPS
230	  service on another port of that host would all receive a
231	  `Secure` cookie set by one of them. A cookie name per `server_id`
232	  avoids the clash between instances. It does not stop another service
233	  on that host from receiving it. `localStorage` is per origin
234	  (scheme, host and port), so it does not have this problem, but any
235	  script on the origin can read it.
236

# Spikes

Throwaway crates and scripts that answered the Spike 0 questions in
`docs/design.md` before any product code was written. Each directory has a
README with the commands run, their output, and a recommendation. They are
kept for reference and are not built by the main crate.

| Dir | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `01-claude-resume` | Can Claude Code sessions be captured and resumed? | Yes: `--session-id <uuid>` at launch, `--resume <uuid>` later from any terminal. Transcripts pruned after 30 days unless `cleanupPeriodDays` is raised. |
| `02-process-host` | tmux or own PTYs? | tmux on a private server: sessions outlive the app, reattach works, ~3 ms round trip. PTY adapter kept as fallback and for tests. |
| `03-session-state` | How to know "waiting on you"? | Claude Code hooks (`PermissionRequest`, `Stop`, `SessionEnd`) via a tiny `switchboard-hook` binary and a Unix socket; OSC 777 text from the raw stream as the hook-free fallback. |
| `05-keychain` | Can secrets live in the Keychain without prompts? | Yes for a bundle signed with a stable identity and identifier: the item ACL is `identifier + certificate`, so rebuilds read silently. Ad-hoc builds prompt per rebuild. |
| `06-pane-size` | Why is the embedded pane wider than the widget? | `window-size manual` ignored the client; `latest` makes the window follow whichever client attached last. Re-applied on launch for servers that outlive the app. |
| `07-clone-session` | Can a session be cloned up to a chosen message? | Yes: copy the transcript prefix before the chosen prompt, substitute a fresh UUID for `sessionId`, save it `0600` beside the original; `--resume <new>` opens the truncated history and the original is untouched. |

With the tick and `pump` in `App::logic`, hidden queries answer in 75 to 103 ms (eframe's 100 ms throttle for invisible windows). The sleep and wake cycle is not yet measured. |

A port is free only if `0.0.0.0`, `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]` all bind: CRA listens on `*`, which a loopback bind does not see. |

The `aws-vault` form and the no-prompt run under Dispatch's launch flags were not run and are left to the owner. |

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

The search turned up consistent answers on the cause, with one conflict on the "proceed anyway" option.

**Cause:** Chromium-based browsers have matched hostnames only against the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) field since Chrome 58 (April 2017) and ignore the Common Name. Modern Chromium-based browsers (Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera) only check the SAN extension when matching a hostname to a certificate. One source says Safari had never accepted CN-only certs. So a self-signed certificate that lacks a SAN entry matching the IP or hostname will fail in both browsers.

**Proceed option:** Sources disagree. A Palo Alto community post says that without a correct SAN, users will not be provided an option to proceed to the URL. An older NethServer thread, by contrast, describes bypassing the warning through the advanced "proceed" exception in Chrome 58. The NethServer reporter also noted that Firefox needed an exception rule. Treat the bypass as unreliable and regenerate the certificate instead.

**Fix:** Reissue the certificate with a SAN entry for the exact IP or name used in the URL. One vendor example uses -addext "subjectAltName=IP:192.168.192.72" with openssl. Note that a SAN for an IP must match the IP in the URL, which is why a cert covering 127.0.0.1 fails when accessed via another address.

The Apple support article is the primary source, and it lists the requirements. Apple says RSA keys in TLS server certificates and issuing CAs need at least 2048 bits, and SHA-1 signatures are no longer accepted for TLS. A DNS name has to appear in the SAN extension, since a CommonName alone no longer gets trust (1-6, 1-7).

For certificates issued after July 1, 2019, Apple adds two rules: an EKU extension with the serverAuth OID (1-8), and a validity period of 825 days or less (1-9). Apple also states that connections to servers that break these rules fail (1-10).

Secondary sources agree. One developer note says the 825-day and serverAuth checks apply in WKWebView and Safari even when the issuing CA is trusted (4-3). Another notes that Chrome doesn't enforce these rules for private CAs, so a non-compliant certificate can work in Chrome but fail on iOS (4-4).

Here's what the search found on both parts of your query.

**Port isolation (RFC 6265):** The RFC's security considerations section says cookies do not isolate by port. A cookie readable or writable by one service on a host is equally readable or writable by a service on another port of that host. A related draft, RFC 6265bis, notes that this differs from the same-origin policy, which does separate content by port. The RFC also advises servers not to run mutually distrusting services on different ports of one host while storing security-sensitive data in cookies.

**SameSite Strict and same-origin WebSockets:** The search did not turn up a browser or spec source that directly confirms a SameSite Strict cookie is sent on a same-origin WebSocket handshake. The closest source is Electron's WebSocket documentation, which says that by default the handshake's Origin matches the WebSocket URL's origin, so the connection is treated as same-origin by SameSite cookie rules. A Strict cookie is generally withheld only from cross-site requests, so a same-site handshake should carry it. That is my inference from the SameSite definition, not something a source stated for WebSockets, so verify it in the browser you target.

The search didn't return RFC 6455's own text on the server-echo rule, so the points below come from secondary sources and should be checked against the RFC itself.

- **Browser behavior:** The WHATWG HTML spec says a WebSocket connection is only established if the server reports that it selected one of the client's requested subprotocols (Each string in the array is a subprotocol name. The connection will only be established if the server reports that it has selected one of these subprotocols.). This is the browser-side basis for the failure you described.
- **Server response:** The http.dev reference says the response header contains a single selected subprotocol name.
- **Token characters:** A Microsoft reference source quotes RFC 6455's requirement that names use characters in the range U+0021 to U+007E, excluding separators defined in RFC 2616, and that all names be unique (MUST be non-empty strings with characters in the range U+0021 to U+007E not including separator characters as defined in [RFC2616], and MUST all be unique strings.). The header value is an ABNF list of tokens (1#token).
- **Registry note:** RFC 7936 says IANA should refuse subprotocol registrations that differ only by case (IANA is, however, instructed to decline registrations in the registry which differ only as to case).
- **Implementation example:** The `ws` library's parser checks each character against a token table and throws a syntax error on unexpected characters, so it enforces the token rules in practice.

To confirm the exact echo requirement, read RFC 6455 Section 4.2.2 directly on rfc-editor.org. The search results did not include that section.

The search turned up a consistent picture: Safari on iOS has a long-standing problem with `wss://` on self-signed certificates, even after the user has accepted the certificate for the page. The results are mostly old (2010 to 2019), so check whether anything has changed in current iOS versions.

- **Accepting the certificate for HTTPS doesn't carry over to WebSocket.** A WebKit bug report from 2011 describes Safari proceeding past the warning for the page and its `https://` requests, while a `wss://` connection to the same host still fails. [WebKit mailing list](https://lists.webkit.org/pipermail/webkit-dev/2011-June/017338.html) The bug was filed as WebKit Bug 41419. [WebKit Bugzilla](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419) One reporter found that setting the certificate to "always trust" made the WebSocket work. [WebKit Bugzilla](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419)
- **The error is typically OSStatus -9807.** A 2019 report on iOS 13 describes this error as meaning an invalid certificate chain. [Cendio bug 7401](https://bugzilla.cendio.com/show_bug.cgi?id=7401) Another report from Turris matches it. [Turris GitLab](https://gitlab.nic.cz/turris/reforis/foris-js/-/merge_requests/154)
- **Certificate requirements matter.** In the Cendio case, adding a Subject Alternative Name was what made the WebSocket work, and the team also flagged Extended Key Usage and certificate validity length as iOS 13 requirements to meet. [Cendio bug 7401](https://bugzilla.cendio.com/show_bug.cgi?id=7401) A WebKit commenter likewise could not get Safari to accept a self-signed certificate without a SAN. [WebKit Bugzilla](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345)
- **Workarounds.** The Cockpit project says the default iOS WebSocket framework won't accept self-signed certificates even when manually trusted, and recommends a valid certificate. As an alternative, it suggests enabling the experimental "NSURLSession WebSocket" option under Safari's Experimental Features. [Cockpit](https://cockpit-project.org/running/safari) The WebKit maintainers said the fix belongs in the embedding application or the browser vendor, and that a click-through bypass for WebSocket is a security concern. [WebKit Bugzilla](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419)

Practical takeaways: make sure the certificate includes a SAN and meets current Apple certificate requirements, or use a publicly trusted certificate. Otherwise, try the experimental NSURLSession WebSocket setting for testing.

**Section 4.1 (client validation of the server's handshake):** If the server's response includes a Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header naming a subprotocol the client didn't request, the client must fail the connection. The spec says the response must not "indicates the use of a subprotocol that was not present in the client's handshake," and the client then "MUST _Fail the WebSocket Connection_."

**Section 4.2.2 (server selecting a subprotocol):** The server must choose from the client's offered values. The spec states that "The value chosen MUST be derived from the client's handshake." If the server supports none of the requested subprotocols, "the only acceptable value is null," and it "MUST NOT send back a Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header field in its response."

The results cover the .local resolution behavior well, but they say little about Safari and the Local Network permission prompt specifically.

**Resolution behavior:** Multicast DNS is the mechanism behind .local names. One source describes the rule as any DNS query for a name ending with the label local must be sent to the mDNS IPv4 link-local multicast address 224.0.0.251, or its IPv6 equivalent FF02::FB. Apple's Bonjour implements this, and it automatically resolves the private IP addresses of link-local Macintosh computers running MacOS and mobile devices running iOS if .local is appended to their hostnames.

**Safari failures:** Several reports describe Safari failing on .local names that depend on unicast DNS. In one 2010 thread, a trace showed that the iPhone4 does NOT query the configured DNS server for .local tlds and thus cannot resolve these host names. A later report says that after an iOS 10 beta, even using the FQDN instead of the shortname in Safari doesn't work, even though the DNS query succeeds. A Versa Networks support article attributes this to Apple's resolver: the system resolver is instructed not to query traditional Unicast DNS servers for any domain ending in .local. The same article says the domain must be explicitly defined in the Search Domains list pushed via the VPN profile. This is a vendor claim, not Apple documentation.

**Local Network permission:** The one Apple-sourced item is a Developer Forums answer about `ProcessInfo.hostName`. A developer reported that it requires 'local network' permission on iOS, and an Apple DTS engineer acknowledged the permission was not documented for that API. The same DTS engineer points to TN3179 "Understanding local network privacy" for guidance. A separate forum thread notes that it's generally best to trigger privacy alerts when the user performs an operation that's obviously associated with the alert.

**Gap:** I found no source that directly confirms whether Safari's own .local lookups trigger the Local Network prompt, or whether a denied permission blocks them. Checking TN3179 would be the next step.

The search didn't turn up anything about the QR code, camera, or certificate-warning part of your query. It only returned material on `history.replaceState` itself and some old iOS security issues.

- **What `replaceState` does:** The replaceState() method of the History interface modifies the current history entry, replacing it with the state object and URL passed in the method parameters. The new URL must be of the same origin as the current URL; otherwise the replaceState() method throws an exception. MDN also notes that it won't cause the browser to load bar2.html or even check that bar2.html exists.
- **Old iOS Safari issues:** CVE-2010-1407 is a flaw in WebKit on iOS before version 4 where it does not properly implement the history.replaceState method in certain situations involving IFRAME elements. A separate issue, CVE-2012-0585, let Private Browsing in Safari on iOS before 5.1 insert history entries via JavaScript code that calls the (1) pushState or (2) replaceState method.

Both CVEs are over a decade old and fixed, so they probably don't explain a current QR-code certificate warning. I found no source linking `replaceState` to QR codes, the iOS camera, or certificate warnings, so that connection remains unverified. The results cover the .local resolution behavior well, but they say little about Safari and the Local Network permission prompt specifically.

**Resolution behavior:** Multicast DNS is the mechanism behind .local names. One source describes the rule as any DNS query for a name ending with the label local must be sent to the mDNS IPv4 link-local multicast address 224.0.0.251, or its IPv6 equivalent FF02::FB. Apple's Bonjour implements this, and it automatically resolves the private IP addresses of link-local Macintosh computers running MacOS and mobile devices running iOS if .local is appended to their hostnames.

**Safari failures:** Several reports describe Safari failing on .local names that depend on unicast DNS. In one 2010 thread, a trace showed that the iPhone4 does NOT query the configured DNS server for .local tlds and thus cannot resolve these host names. A later report says that after an iOS 10 beta, even using the FQDN instead of the shortname in Safari doesn't work, even though the DNS query succeeds. A Versa Networks support article attributes this to Apple's resolver: the system resolver is instructed not to query traditional Unicast DNS servers for any domain ending in .local. The same article says the domain must be explicitly defined in the Search Domains list pushed via the VPN profile. This is a vendor claim, not Apple documentation.

**Local Network permission:** The one Apple-sourced item is a Developer Forums answer about `ProcessInfo.hostName`. A developer reported that it requires 'local network' permission on iOS, and an Apple DTS engineer acknowledged the permission was not documented for that API. The same DTS engineer points to TN3179 "Understanding local network privacy" for guidance. A separate forum thread notes that it's generally best to trigger privacy alerts when the user performs an operation that's obviously associated with the alert.

**Gap:** I found no source that directly confirms whether Safari's own .local lookups trigger the Local Network prompt, or whether a denied permission blocks them. Checking TN3179 would be the next step.

# Facts for issue #230 (browser page on the remote port)

No spike was run. Every open browser question needs a device, a browser or a person's tap, which is not runnable here. Those are under Unresolved or For the owner. `git status` is empty.

## Settled

### The tree
- `RemoteRequest` is built in one place, `src/adapters/remote.rs:506`. Adding `cookie`, `origin`, `user_agent` or `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` fields touches that site only. No test builds it by literal (grep of `src` and `tests`). It is `pub` in `adapters/`, not in `ports/`, so CLAUDE.md's additivity rule for `model.rs`, `action.rs` and `ports/` does not cover it. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:360-372`.
- `RemoteReply` is built as a literal at about 10 sites in `src/app.rs` (for example `:1664`, `:1679`, `:2365-2376`, `:2754`, `:3570`, `:3723`, `:3736`, `:3767`). Most go through `envelope` and `envelope_at` (`:3717-3736`). Adding response headers means changing those literals, or giving the new field a `Default`.
- `last_message` is on the `Stopped` hook event (`src/ports/events.rs:23-24`). It is not a `SessionRecord` field: grep of `src/core/model.rs` finds none. It is not on `SessionView` either (investigation notes, `control/src/lib.rs:636-688`). `docs/remote-client.md:207` says the card excerpt is "`last_message` ... a field of the session's metadata", and the tree does not back that. The plan must either add an excerpt field or fetch `last-response` per session, as the headset does.
- The certificate has no SAN and a year-4096 `not_after`. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:91-92` and investigation notes l.45-56 (`CertificateParams::new(Vec::new())`).
- `PairingInvite.parse` decodes JSON only: `client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:93-116`. `addresses` is `[String]`.
- `addresses` is used as a list in `client/Tests/SwitchboardProtocolTests/FixturesTests.swift:159-164`, and in the `PairingInvite(...)` initialisers in `ReconcileTests`, `WatchTests`, `DraftTests`, `CommandTests`, `EventTests`, `TicketTests` and `NewSessionTests` under `client/Tests/SwitchboardClientCoreTests`.
- Non-test users of `PairingInvite`: `ConnectionManager.swift`, `BrowserView.swift`, `switchboard-remote/main.swift`. So the URL-first, JSON-fallback parser and the `addresses` list can be kept additively.
- Cookies are not isolated by port, so a `Secure` cookie set by one Switchboard instance reaches other services on the same host. Evidence: RFC 6265 §8.5 and §8.6 (reported by the search below; the RFC page itself was not fetched). Combined with the investigation's point that `localStorage` is per origin, this is a fact the plan can use for decision 2.

### Certificates and browsers (vendor documentation)
- Apple requires, for iOS 13 and macOS 10.15 and later, that a TLS server certificate carry the server's DNS name in the SAN extension, as the CN alone is not trusted. For certificates issued after 2019-07-01 it must also contain an EKU with `id-kp-serverAuth` and have a validity of 825 days or fewer. https://support.apple.com/103769 (fetched; quoted). So a year-4096 `not_after` fails Apple's rule for a certificate trusted on a device. This covers iOS 13 and macOS 10.15 onward, and Apple's page names no later change.
  - Queries: "Apple requirements for trusted certificates in iOS 13 and macOS 10.15 825 days SAN serverAuth".
- Chromium has matched hostnames only against the SAN, ignoring the CN, since Chrome 58 (2017). A certificate whose SAN lacks the IP or name in the URL gives `ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID`. Sources: https://dev.to/dimastopel/why-subject-alternative-names-sans-matter-for-modern-browsers-30p0 and https://cert-depot.com/guides/why-sans-matter, two secondary agreeing sources. A WebKit comment in https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345 could not get Safari to accept a self-signed certificate without a SAN. The planner should build to a reissued certificate with a SAN for the address.
  - Queries: "self-signed certificate without subjectAltName IP address Chrome Safari NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID proceed anyway".
- On iOS and iPadOS Safari, `wss://` to a self-signed or invalid certificate fails even when the certificate is manually trusted. Cockpit's documentation says so (https://cockpit-project.org/running/safari, fetched). WebKit bug 41419 is still NEW, last modified 2026-01-12 (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419, fetched): Safari's WebSocket stack did not take the user's exception. Turris and Cendio report OSStatus -9807 until SAN, EKU and validity were fixed (https://gitlab.nic.cz/turris/reforis/foris-js/-/merge_requests/154, https://bugzilla.cendio.com/show_bug.cgi?id=7401). Cockpit offers the experimental "NSURLSession WebSocket" flag as a workaround, and its page names no iOS version. Two sources agree and the vendor's bug is open and unfixed, so the behaviour exists. The plan must not rely on `new WebSocket` working on iOS after a click-through. This also settles that the click-through is not trust for WebSocket traffic on iOS Safari, where installing a compliant certificate as trusted is the route that has worked in the reports.
  - Queries: "Safari iOS self-signed certificate accepted click-through WebSocket wss fails fetch works"; "Safari iOS WebSocket self-signed certificate NSURLSession WebSocket experimental feature wss untrusted certificate".

### WebSocket and cookies (standards)
- A `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` value must come from the client's offered list: the server may only select one the client offered, and a client fails the connection when the server names one it did not request or when it asked for subprotocols and none is selected. RFC 6455 §4.1 and §4.2.2 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.html, fetched; only the first 100000 of 176684 characters were read, and both sections are inside that). The WHATWG HTML spec says the connection is established only if the server selects one of the offered values (reported by search, not fetched). Values are tokens, U+0021 to U+007E excluding separators. So a token-in-subprotocol design needs the host to echo the value in the 101 (`respond_upgrade`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`, writes none today), and it puts the token in a request header the host's access logs and proxies may see.
  - Queries: "RFC 6455 Sec-WebSocket-Protocol server must echo subprotocol otherwise browser fails connection; token characters".
- A browser cannot set headers on `new WebSocket()`: the issue states this and the API takes only URL and subprotocols. WHATWG WebSockets standard (not fetched; common knowledge, so not relied on).

## Unresolved

### U1. Does a click-through exception cover `fetch` and `wss://` in each browser?
- Tried: the queries above plus "Chrome self-signed certificate warning bypass remembered how long proceed exception per host Chromium SSL error allowlist". Result: the iOS WebSocket failure is settled above. For `fetch` in Safari, and for Chrome and Firefox WebSocket, no primary source was found. WebKit bug 41419 comment 3 says Chrome accepted the same server. Chrome's retention of exceptions is reported as one week by Paessler and "a few days" by HPE. Both are vendor support pages for third-party products, not Chromium, so it is not settled. Firefox and Safari retention were not found.
- Build to: a page that works over `fetch` alone. Live updates fall back to polling `GET waiting` and the open session's `last-response` every few seconds when the socket fails or does not open within 5 s. If the answer is favourable, the socket is a faster path on top. If unfavourable, the polling path is the page, and "moves to the top without a reload" still holds. Whatever the answer, the plan must add a SAN to the certificate and bound its validity, and test the reissue (see For the owner, O3).

### U2. Does a click-through page count as a secure context (`crypto.randomUUID`, `Secure` cookies)?
- Tried: "secure context page loaded over HTTPS with certificate error click through crypto.randomUUID isSecureContext". Only MDN (randomUUID is secure-context-only) and an old Mozilla bug (https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1162772: Chrome rejected a service worker over a self-signed certificate, Firefox allowed it). Nothing on `isSecureContext` after a bypass.
- Build to: generate the op id with `crypto.getRandomValues`, which is not secure-context-gated (reported by the same search; MDN). Don't depend on `randomUUID`. If favourable, `randomUUID` may be used. If unfavourable, nothing changes. For the cookie, a `Secure` cookie on a bypassed origin is the same unknown, so decision 2 should carry a fallback: the cookie with the token also returned in the `/pair` body (the page already receives it) and a socket opened with the subprotocol path on failure.

### U3. Are `SameSite=Strict` cookies sent on a same-origin `new WebSocket()` handshake, and does `Secure` work for an IP host?
- Tried: "RFC 6265 cookies do not isolate by port; SameSite Strict cookie sent on same-origin WebSocket handshake"; "WebSocket handshake cookies SameSite Strict same-origin sent Chrome Safari Firefox cookie header upgrade request". Leads only: an Apple developer forum thread (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/104488) and WebKit bug 232666 (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=232666) report Strict cookies not sent on Safari WebSockets in restored or cached tabs, with a fix around Safari 15.1 per the report. Chrome and Firefox: no primary source. Nothing found on `Secure` for IP-address hosts.
- Build to: the host accepts the bearer header, the cookie, and the subprotocol token, in that order, behind one `authenticate`. If the cookie works in a browser, the page's script never holds the token. If not, the page stores the token and uses the subprotocol. Use `SameSite=Lax` only if the owner accepts it, since Strict is the issue's stated choice.

### U4. Is the URL with the code kept in history, tab list or iCloud tab sync before `replaceState` runs? Does `replaceState` remove it from history?
- Tried: "history.replaceState replaces current session history entry URL; iOS Safari camera QR code opens link certificate warning history". Only MDN: `replaceState` modifies the current history entry. Nothing on browsers' separate stores, and nothing on a certificate interstitial that appears before any page script runs.
- Build to: the code is one-time and expires in five minutes or three wrong tries (`src/core/remote.rs:46-73`), so a leaked URL after the window closes is inert. The plan states that the URL exists in the browser's records until the interstitial passes and the page replaces it, and says so in the dialog. If the interstitial never gets past, the code is still in history, which the window's expiry bounds. Do not claim the code never reaches history.

### U5. Does `.local` resolve from iOS Safari?
- Tried: "iOS Safari resolves .local mDNS hostname Bonjour local network permission Safari". Apple forum and a vendor article say `.local` is resolved by multicast only, and that unicast lookups are skipped. Nothing on Safari and the Local Network prompt (Apple's TN3179 was not fetched).
- Build to: the URL host is the IP from `local_address()`, bracketed if IPv6. A `.local` second QR is a later add if the answer is favourable.

### U6. How many parallel connections does iOS Safari open per host, and how long does it keep an idle one?
- Not searched (the query budget went to the certificate and WebSocket questions); no source in hand.
- Build to: the page loads three files at most (`/`, one script, one stylesheet), so a first load needs three connections of the unauthenticated pool of four. If unfavourable, answer static paths from the connection thread with `Connection: close`, so they free the slot at once. The plan should do that anyway since static bytes need no core state.

## For the owner

- O1. On a real iPhone and a Mac, after the SAN-bearing certificate is accepted by click-through: does the page load, does `fetch` return, does `new WebSocket` open, and is `isSecureContext` true? Favourable: the socket path stays primary. Unfavourable: polling is the path, and the dialog says to install the certificate as trusted for live updates. The plan builds both, so it never waits on this.
- O2. Which browsers must work: iOS Safari only, or also Chrome and Firefox? Fact the owner holds that the tree does not: which devices they own. Either answer: build to a page that works on `fetch` alone.
- O3. Can the identity certificate be reissued over the existing key so `spki_sha256` is unchanged? `make_identity` makes a new key today (investigation l.246). That is a fact about the Keychain-held key and `identity.json`, checkable in the tree by reading `src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127` and the Keychain adapter. It is not settled by a source and was not read to the end here. If it can, existing paired devices keep their pin. If it cannot, a reissue rotates the key and every paired device must pair again, which the plan states in the changelog.
- O4. Whether the owner's phone shows the camera's link preview for a URL with a self-signed certificate at all (iOS camera banner behaviour). Favourable: scan opens the page. Unfavourable: the dialog's text copy of the URL is the path, which the plan builds anyway.

Response headers (CSP, Set-Cookie, Content-Type) need a field with a default or edits to those sites.

The plan adds an excerpt field or fetches `last-response` per session, as the headset does.
